project.name: Smatchet
project.description: Smatchet is a high-performance, engine-agnostic productivity tool and issue-tracking client that unifies project management, Perforce source-control analysis, and AI assistance behind a single Dear ImGui interface built on C++14. It supports multiple tracker backends (Jira and Plane.so) through a backend-agnostic architecture and ships as both a standalone desktop application (GLFW + OpenGL3) and an embedded plugin for Unreal Engine (DX12). Note: this project has over 100 source files; consider scoping analysis to a subdirectory for faster results.

tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: Start with the README to understand what Smatchet is and why it exists: a C++14 + Dear ImGui productivity client that unifies multi-backend issue tracking (Jira, Plane.so, GitHub), Perforce annotate, SQLite caching, optional Lua automation, and an MCP server. The README also names the two deployment targets that everything else in this tour hangs off — a standalone GLFW/OpenGL desktop app and an Unreal Engine DX12 plugin — and points at the directory split (`Source_Core/`, `Target_Standalone/`, `Plugins/`, `UnrealPlugins/`) that mirrors the layers we'll walk through next.

tour.title: Standalone Entry Point
tour.description: The standalone executable bootstraps from a single `main.cpp` that wires GLFW + OpenGL, initializes Dear ImGui, prepares the runtime asset and user-data directories, registers the optional MCP, Lua and Whisper plugins with the plugin host, and runs the per-frame draw loop. This is the highest-fan-out node in the BFS (depth 0) and the cleanest place to see how the layers we tour next get stitched together at startup. It also delegates CLI invocations (`smatchet cmd ...`) to a separate `CliCommandRunner` so the same binary can run headless against the command registry from Step 8.
tour.languageLesson: C++14 hard target (Unreal compat): no `string_view`, no `optional`, no `if constexpr`. The entry point must compile under both MinGW UCRT (standalone) and MSVC (Unreal plugin), which is why every owned object is an explicit `std::unique_ptr` rather than relying on newer move-semantics shortcuts.

tour.title: AppController — The Orchestrator
tour.description: `AppController` is the top-level non-UI object owned by `main.cpp`. It composes the tracker backend (Step 5), the local SQLite cache (Step 6), the AI assistant (Step 9), the Lua automation host, and the merge-watch notification server — so every other layer routes through here. With a fan-in of 88, it is the third-most-referenced node in the codebase (after `Logger.h` and `ConfigManager.h`), which makes its public header the de-facto contract every subsystem implicitly depends on. `ConfigManager` is its persistent settings backend (tracker creds, AI keys, theme prefs, view layouts) and uses `nlohmann/json_fwd` deliberately to keep the JSON template explosion out of every translation unit.

tour.title: Core Foundations — Logging, Cache, Threading
tour.description: Three pieces of plumbing show up in nearly every translation unit. `Logger.h` is the most-included header in the project (fan-in 96): a leveled logger with an in-memory ring buffer for the Log panel UI and an async file-sink worker thread, so no caller ever blocks on disk I/O. `LocalCacheManager` is the SQLite-backed cache for field catalogs, tickets, and pending-mutation queues — the layer that keeps Smatchet usable offline and snappy when the tracker REST API is slow. `MainThreadDispatcher` is the canonical worker-to-UI hand-off mandated by Pillar 2 (UI never freezes): workers `PostToMainThread()` and the per-frame draw loop drains the queue, so UI state is only ever mutated from the UI thread.
tour.languageLesson: Pillar 2 hard rule: any synchronous call to cpr / SQLite / p4 / `std::ifstream` / `std::mutex::lock` reachable from an `ImGui::*` frame is a code-review CRITICAL. The `MainThreadDispatcher` pattern (lock-free SPSC-style queue drained from the UI thread each frame) is how every worker safely returns its result without touching ImGui state directly.

tour.title: Tracker Abstraction — One Interface, Many Backends
tour.description: The README's headline feature is multi-backend tracker support, and the seam that makes it work is `ITrackerClient` — a single interface declaring the full issue/field/sprint/comment/worklog API surface that every consumer (UI, command system, AI) talks to. `ITrackerBackendFactory` picks the concrete backend (Jira, GitHub, Plane) from runtime configuration, so swapping tracker is a Preferences-panel toggle rather than a recompile. `TrackerFieldSchema` defines the canonical shape of fields, components, users, projects, and create-meta — the lingua franca that backends translate their native API into so the UI doesn't care which tracker it's pointed at.

tour.title: Concrete Tracker Backends
tour.description: Three implementations of `ITrackerClient` sit behind the factory from Step 5. `JiraClient` is the most mature (the project started Jira-only) and hits the Jira REST API; `PlaneClient` targets Plane.so with caching for project listings; `GitHubClient` is the newest, hitting the GitHub Issues REST API. They share `TrackerHttpUtils` (auth headers, URL building, timeouts) so cross-cutting concerns like rate-limit handling, retry, and PAT-vs-OAuth header shaping aren't reinvented per backend. Each runs its HTTP calls on worker threads and posts results back via the dispatcher from Step 4 — never the UI thread.

tour.title: Sync, Offline Queue, and Drafts
tour.description: Backends from Step 6 are wrapped by two services that make Smatchet usable when the network isn't. `TicketSyncService` drives streaming fetch packs, deletion bookkeeping, and pending-sync coalescing so the grid keeps up with large projects without UI hitches. `OfflineQueueService` stores ticket create/edit operations while the network is down, retrying on reconnect and dead-lettering on terminal failure. `IssueDraft` is the in-progress data model for issue creation — field values, attachments, pending state — drafted locally and submitted through the queue when the backend is reachable.

tour.title: UI Surface — ImGui Orchestrator and Per-Frame Session
tour.description: Above the core sits an engine-agnostic Dear ImGui surface that both the standalone exe and the Unreal plugin render. `SmatchetUI` is the top-level orchestrator — it owns the main menu bar, Preferences, Views Dashboard, Active Project, Bulk Import/Export, Audit, and Log windows, and dispatches per-frame draw work. `SmatchetUiSession` is the giant per-frame `UiDrawSession` struct holding every transient buffer, modal toggle, async future, and queued edit threaded through every draw helper — a deliberate single-owner pattern that avoids spreading mutable UI state across globals. `TicketGridModel` and `Views` back the grid: column metadata, field-by-id lookup, and the persisted user-view set (column ordering, filters, tracker bindings) with revision tracking.
tour.languageLesson: Dear ImGui is immediate-mode: there is no retained widget tree. Every frame, the UI thread walks `SmatchetUI::Draw` top to bottom, calling `ImGui::Begin/End`, `ImGui::Button`, etc. The `UiDrawSession` struct holds the across-frame state (text buffers, selection, modal toggles) that the IM API itself doesn't retain, while ImGui's own `ImGuiContext` retains layout/focus/IO. This is why `SmatchetUiSession.h` is fan-in 40 — almost every draw helper takes it by reference.

tour.title: Command System — One Registry, Four Frontends
tour.description: The README brags about 56+ named commands surfaced through CLI, Command Palette, MCP, and Lua via one registry — this is where that lives. `Command` defines the unified struct (params, error codes, result/context types) that every frontend speaks. `CommandRegistry` is the global singleton storing every Command and providing lookup/enumerate/invoke entry points (fan-in 35). `CommandPaletteUi` is the Ctrl+Shift+P modal frontend with fuzzy search, recents prioritization, keyboard navigation, and inline parameter forms — the same registry is also walked by `CliCommandRunner` (Step 2), the MCP plugin (Step 11), and the Lua bindings.

tour.title: AI Assistant — Worker-Thread Streaming
tour.description: The Ctrl+Shift+A side panel from the README is backed by `AiAssistantController`, a worker-thread coordinator that orchestrates streaming LLM calls off the UI thread per Pillar 2. `IAiClient` is the provider-neutral interface (concrete clients exist for OpenAI, Anthropic, and Ollama under `Source_Core/src/`), and `AiTypes` holds the POD types every layer shares: `AiProvider`, `AiMessage`, `AiChatRequest`, `AiStreamDelta`, `AiContextBlock`, plus the cancel-token alias used to abort an in-flight stream when the user hits the cancel button.

tour.title: Plugin Host — Optional Lua, MCP, and Whisper
tour.description: Smatchet's three optional features (Lua automation, MCP server, push-to-talk dictation) ship as static plugins behind a common `IPlugin` lifecycle (OnEarlyInit / OnStart / OnDraw / OnStop). `PluginHost` (declared in `Source_Core/`) is the container that registers them and dispatches lifecycle events — registered by `main.cpp` back in Step 2. `McpPlugin` hosts the HTTP/JSON-RPC server that lets external tools (Claude Code, IDE integrations) drive the command registry from Step 9. `LuaConsolePlugin` provides the in-app Lua 5.3 console (script browser, syntax-highlighted editor, REPL) for the sol2-bound automation surface. `WhisperPlugin` registers global push-to-talk hotkeys and runs the Whisper transcription pipeline.
tour.languageLesson: Plugin gating uses preprocessor flags: `#if SMATCHET_WITH_LUA_AUTOMATION` / `#if SMATCHET_WITH_MCP`. When a plugin is off, a `*_LuaStubs.cpp` translation unit replaces the real bindings TU to keep the symbol surface stable — a C++14-friendly alternative to feature-flag templates that compile-time disappears in stripped builds.

tour.title: CI and Performance Gates
tour.description: Smatchet's UX Pillars (sustain 144 Hz, never freeze, never crash) are not aspirations — they are enforced by CI. `build-and-test.yml` is the primary CI workflow building under `ninja-test-msys2` and running the doctest unit rig on every push and PR (scoped via `paths-ignore` for doc-only diffs). `perf-pr-fast.yml` is the per-PR perf gate: it runs the scenario subset implicated by the diff against `docs/perf/baselines/`, auto-bootstraps the `ci-windows-latest` baseline on first run, and **fails** subsequent PRs that regress beyond the thresholds in `regression-policy.json`. Together they enforce Pillars 1 + 3 as merge gates rather than as documentation.
tour.languageLesson: YAML CI gotcha — GitHub Actions evaluates `paths-ignore` on the workflow file itself, not per-job. The `build-and-test.yml` skip on pure-docs diffs (`docs/**`, `*.md`) cuts CI runner cost for documentation PRs to zero while the perf gate keeps a separate trigger set focused on source paths. Baselines live per-host (dev vs ci-windows-latest) because absolute timings vary between hardware — only relative regression is compared.
